Lindsay Clancy’s former psychiatrist faces tense day of questioning in murder trial

Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, questioned Dr. Jennifer Tufts for hours Monday under cross-examination.

By Abby Patkin

updated on August 10, 2026
14 minutes to read

On the stand Monday:

  • Julie Paul, psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner
  • Dr. Jennifer Tufts

This story may contain content readers find disturbing. For help with postpartum mood disorders, text or call 1-833-TLC-MAMA for the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, call 988 or go to https://988lifeline.org/ to chat online.

5:30 p.m. update: Psychiatric NP who treated Lindsay Clancy explains importance of patient buy-in with medications

Lindsay Clancy’s screening at South Shore Hospital’s Perinatal Behavioral Health Program indicated she was experiencing “extreme” anxiety, according to Julie Paul, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who treated her there in November 2022. 

Paul testified that Clancy also scored a 23 out of 30 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, though crucially, she was negative for suicidality. 

Advertisement:

Paul, who launched the Perinatal Behavioral Health Program in 2018, explained that she met Clancy in late November through Clancy’s then-mother-in-law, Sue, who also worked as a nurse at South Shore Hospital. Paul testified that she called Clancy — who had given birth to her third child about six months prior — and determined she would be a good candidate for the perinatal program.

“She said she did really well for the first 12 weeks [after giving birth]. She was excited, really happy,” Paul recalled. “And then when Patrick [Clancy’s then-husband] went back to work, she said she started to struggle with some anxiety.” 

Advertisement:

Clancy had been working with a psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, and tried a few different psychiatric medications, to varying degrees of success. According to Paul, Clancy had also visited the South Shore Hospital emergency room a few days prior, on Nov. 16, 2022. 

“I asked her specifically if she felt like she wanted to harm herself or her children, and she said no,” Paul testified. She said Clancy also denied having auditory or visual hallucinations at the time.

The young mother also reported struggling with anxiety following the birth of her second child, Paul recalled. Asked if Clancy had been able to manage that earlier bout of anxiety without medication, Paul replied, “as far as what I was told, yes.” However, Tufts previously testified that Clancy briefly tried the antidepressant Zoloft after her second pregnancy. 

Paul told jurors she decided to start Clancy on the antidepressant Prozac, which Clancy had previously been prescribed while in nursing school. She explained that Prozac can temporarily worsen anxiety before it alleviates symptoms, so she opted to pair it with Ativan, a benzodiazepine, to ensure Clancy was more comfortable and able to sleep. 

Answering a question from prosecutors, Paul explained that side effects generally occur within the first week or two on Prozac, though it takes four to six weeks for patients to feel better. Clancy was nervous about starting Prozac, so Paul testified that she encouraged Clancy to stick with the plan. 

Advertisement:

But on Nov. 25, 2022 — three days into taking Prozac — Clancy reported she wasn’t tolerating the medication and was feeling disconnected and “out of it,” Paul said. 

Paul testified that she opted to discontinue the Prozac and prescribe a one-time dose of Ambien to help Clancy sleep, alongside a prescription for mirtazapine, or Remeron, another antidepressant that “works really good for sedation and anxiety.” She paired the drugs with Klonopin, a longer-acting benzodiazepine intended to help Clancy with her sleep and anxiety as she started the new antidepressant.

Paul also noted that she warned Clancy against taking Ativan and Klonopin at the same time. Clancy, she added, was “really anxious” about being dependent on benzodiazepines.

Asked if she had concerns about Clancy stopping Prozac after only three days, Paul replied, “When a client doesn’t have buy-in to the medication, it’s awful. It doesn’t work as well.”

She continued: “I was working with Lindsay to try and find a medication that would make her feel more comfortable. She was feeling very uncomfortable, very anxious. And the Prozac, she just wasn’t tolerating the activation from the Prozac.”

Advertisement:

Paul agreed it is “pretty common practice” in psychiatry to try different medications to find the right one for a given patient. She said she also recommended that Clancy consider a partial hospitalization program at Rhode Island’s Women & Infants Hospital Center for Women’s Behavioral Health but that Clancy felt at the time it wouldn’t work logistically for her family. 

Paul told jurors she ultimately transferred Clancy’s care to another provider on Nov. 30, 2022, because she was already in the process of leaving her job for an out-of-state move. 

Judge William Sullivan ended Monday’s court session at about 3:50 p.m. after Paul’s direct examination by prosecutors. She is expected back on the stand Tuesday morning to undergo cross-examination. 

3:45 p.m. update: Lindsay Clancy’s former psychiatrist, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, finishes testimony

Lindsay Clancy’s former psychiatrist faced a blistering cross-examination Monday as Clancy’s defense attorney sought to cast doubt on her training and expertise, her due diligence, and the thoroughness of her care as she treated Clancy’s postpartum mental illness. 

Attorney Kevin Reddington emphasized that Dr. Jennifer Tufts had only been practicing independently — and with her full credentials — for about a month before she began working with Clancy in September 2022. Tufts, for her part, said she treated “many” postpartum patients during her residency and had specific training with that population, including a specialized elective with a perinatal psychiatrist. 

Reddington turned his attention to postpartum psychosis, a severe condition Clancy alleges she experienced when she killed her three children in January 2023. 

Advertisement:

Tufts said she did not treat any postpartum psychosis patients in the month or so before she began seeing Clancy, explaining that it is “a very rare disorder.” However, she agreed with Reddington that postpartum psychosis is a “legitimate” diagnosis that can result in patients hearing voices in their heads, as Clancy says she did. 

Judge William Sullivan overruled prosecutors’ objection as Reddington noted that Tufts is a named defendant in “a very large lawsuit,” likely referring to Clancy’s malpractice suit against several of her mental health care providers. (Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, has also named Tufts and others in a separate wrongful death lawsuit.)

“And you know that the outcome of this case is very, very major to the outcome of your lawsuit?” Reddington pressed. 

“I don’t actually know that,” Tufts shot back. 

Reddington then asked Tufts whether she would consider it negligent or a misrepresentation to advertise her expertise in perinatal mental health when she was still fresh out of residency. 

“I do not believe that I have been negligent,” Tufts replied. 

Lindsay Clancy’s attorney keeps focus on psychiatrist’s due diligence

Throughout his questioning, Reddington repeatedly noted that Tufts only ever met with Clancy remotely over the course of her treatment, never coming face-to-face until the murder trial. He seemed to suggest telemedicine is somehow deficient or unable to paint the full picture of a patient’s mental distress, a notion prosecutors rejected in their later redirect examination. 

Advertisement:

Reddington also appeared exasperated as Tufts testified about taking Clancy at her word regarding symptoms and medical history, without getting in touch with her family or other providers. When asked about Clancy’s previous use of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, or SSRI antidepressant, for example, Tufts testified that Clancy “said that she took it for a period of time. She didn’t mention any side effects.” 

“Oh, she didn’t tell you that she had side effects. I see,” Reddington sniped. “So when a patient comes to see you with a month under your belt, and they’re sick, and they’re looking for help, you wait for them to volunteer facts to you?”

Tufts maintained that Clancy volunteered “a lot” of information in their sessions and remained able to advocate for herself over the months ahead. 

“She knew very well what her medical history was and was able to provide that for me,” the psychiatrist added. 

Answering another question from Reddington, Tufts said she didn’t administer the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale but instead used another assessment to gauge Clancy’s symptoms of depression. 

“It’s not my choice; that’s the practice at Aster [Mental Health] of what we use,” Tufts testified in response to a later question from prosecutors. Reddington noted that Clancy registered severe depression when evaluated with the Edinburgh scale. 

Advertisement:

Asked what sort of therapy she provided Clancy, Tufts replied, “I listened to her. I listened to her concerns and provided support. I tried to provide her with hope that eventually, things would improve.” 

She defended her decision to prescribe Clancy the SSRI antidepressant Zoloft, describing it as “a top choice, a first-line medication” and a “very effective medication for generalized anxiety disorder.” Reddington, meanwhile, pointed to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s “black box warning” for Zoloft, which warns of a potential increase in suicidal thoughts for certain demographics.  

In one particularly tense line of questioning, Reddington criticized Tufts’s notes on the side effects Clancy experienced after previously taking Zoloft following the birth of her second child. Tufts again defended herself, explaining that Clancy’s prior side effects did not sound severe and she therefore didn’t feel it necessary to document the specific symptoms. 

Tufts also testified that she advised Clancy to discontinue Zoloft in October 2022 when she reported feeling “awful” after about a week on the drug. At the time, Tufts confirmed, Clancy’s side effects included insomnia, diarrhea, loss of appetite, depressed mood, and mental fog, among other symptoms. 

“That must have given you concern that you had a pretty sick patient on your hands at that point, right?” Reddington asked. 

“I was concerned, yes,” Tufts agreed. Answering a question from Reddington, she said Clancy was on a low enough dose of Zoloft that she didn’t need to wean herself off the medication gradually.

Advertisement:

Psychiatrist says she was surprised Lindsay Clancy called suicide hotline

Clancy reported feeling “hopeless” and “close” to having suicidal thoughts by the start of December in 2022, though Tufts said she denied having a plan to harm herself. Still, Tufts agreed with Reddington that patients sometimes minimize their symptoms. 

Reddington also confirmed that Tufts is a mandated reporter, someone required by law to report potential cases of abuse or neglect. 

“And if she told you, ‘I’m having suicidal thoughts; I’m close to it.’ … You’d report that, wouldn’t you?” he asked. 

“Not necessarily,” Tufts answered. “I think it really depends on the context. But having suicidal thoughts alone is not a reportable condition.”

Reddington asked if it would surprise Tufts to know that Clancy called a suicide hotline twice while she was in Tufts’s care. 

“It does surprise me, yes,” Tufts replied. “It surprises me that she called them twice.”

Voice quiet, she said she didn’t think she ever asked whether Clancy had called a suicide hotline. 

“I understand,” Reddington replied, in one of the softer moments of his cross-examination. “You’re a doctor and you were trying to do the right thing … This is just horrible.”

But he continued to lob questions at Tufts, digging into Clancy’s worsening symptoms and poring over the laundry list of medications she was prescribed. He highlighted in particular Clancy’s hesitation to try certain prescriptions due to concerns about side effects.

Advertisement:

“She wasn’t doctor-shopping and asking you to give her drugs so she could get high,” Reddington noted. “She was asking you for help, isn’t that right?”

“Yes,” Tufts confirmed. 

Tufts also testified that she looked into Zulresso — a postpartum depression treatment delivered intravenously under hospital supervision — as a potential option for Clancy, though she said it’s not something she could prescribe outpatient. She said she advised Clancy to discuss Zulresso with providers at Rhode Island’s Women & Infants Hospital Center for Women’s Behavioral Health, where Clancy went for evaluation in December 2022.

In another line of questioning about peer-reviewed articles, Tufts testified that she has published something brief on postpartum mental health. However, she identified herself as a clinician, not a researcher. Reddington pointed to a 2021 article linking thyroid function to postpartum psychosis, and Tufts testified that there was no clinical reason to test Clancy’s thyroid. 

Lindsay Clancy’s attorney accused psychiatrist of pushing her ‘over the edge’

Reddington turned his attention back to Clancy’s Dec. 1, 2022, appointment, when she reported feeling hopeless, unable to sleep, and like she didn’t “care if she dies.” 

“I told her that this was something that we could address, that there was hope, that there were treatments, and there are, you know, different types of treatment programs that are more supportive, like partial hospitalization programs,” Tufts recalled. “So she knew that she still had options and a reason to hope.”

Advertisement:

She said she and Clancy also discussed bipolar disorder in light of Clancy’s insomnia and “extreme” reaction to SSRIs, though Tufts said she ruled out the diagnosis because Clancy “never had mania.” 

“Did you know that around that time, she confessed to her husband that she was having … thoughts of harming her children?” Reddington asked. 

“No,” Tufts replied, adding that she would have been “very concerned” had Clancy told her as much.

At Reddington’s prompting, she confirmed she spoke to Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick, once during one of Clancy’s telemedicine appointments. 

“He said she wasn’t doing well” and felt her deterioration stemmed from Seroquel, an antipsychotic Clancy had been prescribed, Tufts explained. 

Reddington pressed her on whether she remembered Patrick saying the medications were “turning [Clancy] into a zombie,” and she agreed it was possible.

Tufts testified that she advised Clancy to seek out a partial hospitalization program and to visit an emergency room if she had suicidal thoughts or felt she was at risk of hurting herself or others.

During an appointment on Jan. 23, 2023 — one day before the killings — Clancy appeared “depressed and flat,” Tufts agreed. 

“She also reported that her heart was racing, right?” Reddington asked. “She had no motivation, that’s what she told you, right?” 

Yes, Tufts confirmed. She previously testified that Clancy also reported starting the antidepressant amitriptyline, but that it didn’t appear she was experiencing any side effects. 

Advertisement:

“I thought about how I could best help her, the medicines that she’d tried and what her current symptoms were,” Tufts said Monday. “And it made sense to slowly titrate the amitriptyline so that we could get her to a dose that reduced her depression so that she would feel better.” 

“But you increased the amitriptyline?” Reddington confirmed. “That pushed her over the edge, didn’t it?” 

Tufts took a beat before answering, “I don’t think so.” 

As Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague stepped up for redirect examination, Tufts testified that she did not recommend Clancy go to a hospital for evaluation on Jan. 23, 2023, because she was “completely denying” suicidal or homicidal thoughts.

“There were no signs of psychosis or mania, so there were no serious signs that her safety or that anyone else’s safety was at risk,” Tufts added. 

“And during that session, did she ever tell you that she planned to harm herself or the children?” Sprague asked. 

“No,” Tufts maintained. 

Sprague also brought out a bottle of amitriptyline that was prescribed to Clancy on Jan. 16, 2023, and filled the same day. She noted that eight pills were missing, suggesting Clancy didn’t increase her dose as prescribed on the 24th. 

In another line of questioning, Sprague asked whether psychiatrists reach out to patients’ friends and family to discuss their treatment, especially when the patient is able to advocate for themselves.

Advertisement:

“No,” Tufts answered. “In fact, we don’t have HIPAA [Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act] permission to do that.” 

With Tufts still on the stand, Reddington returned for a final round of questions. Smiling slyly, he had Tufts read from her notes on Clancy’s Oct. 21, 2022, appointment, where Tufts had written, “not hyper, pressured speech” — a symptom that can indicate bipolar mania. 

Tufts, however, maintained that she had meant to write that Clancy’s speech was “not pressured.” 

“I know it doesn’t say ‘not,’ but that is exactly what I meant,” Tufts testified. “I don’t care what it says; I know what I meant.” 

Lindsay Clancy‘s murder trial enters its third week Monday with Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Clancy’s former psychiatrist, back on the stand under cross-examination.

Fielding questions from prosecutors Friday, Tufts testified that Clancy appeared “depressed and flat” the day before she strangled her three children and attempted suicide at home in Duxbury on Jan. 24, 2023. At prosecutors’ prompting, Tufts also told jurors Clancy repeatedly denied having suicidal or homicidal thoughts in the months leading up to the killings.

More on Lindsay Clancy:

  • DA’s office says prosecutor’s ‘hot mic’ moment in Lindsay Clancy trial was misheard

  • Lindsay Clancy was ‘depressed and flat’ the day before she killed her children, psychiatrist says

  • Lindsay Clancy’s friends and former father-in-law testify in her murder trial

Clancy, now 35, doesn’t deny she killed 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan. However, she’s raising what’s commonly known as an insanity defense as she argues she can’t be held criminally responsible because she was wracked by postpartum mental illness and heard a voice in her head telling her to kill.

Advertisement:

Clancy’s lawyer has pointed to her numerous psychiatric medications as a contributing factor in her downward spiral. Yet Tufts — who treated Clancy between September 2022 and January 2023 — testified Friday that Clancy was “generally reluctant” to try medications for her mental health and told Tufts in one session, “I keep reaching out to different people and not sticking with the plan.”

Tufts further opined that Clancy had a tendency to over-attribute some of her symptoms to medication side effects. She testified that Clancy reached out to her on Jan. 11, 2023, to ask about ketamine therapy, and while Tufts thought it could be a good fit for Clancy, “I didn’t think we were at that point yet.” 

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague also confirmed Clancy told Tufts around that point that she was “getting desperate for something that would work quickly” to get her out of her depressed state. 

Tufts, who is also a defendant in Clancy’s medical malpractice lawsuit, testified that her initial diagnosis was generalized anxiety disorder and an adjustment disorder with depressed mood, or a reaction to a particular life event that may fall short of the criteria for, say, major depressive disorder.

Tufts told jurors she also raised the possibility of bipolar disorder — a condition with which Clancy has since been diagnosed — but that Clancy “really didn’t meet the criteria” at the time.

Another psychiatrist named in Clancy’s malpractice lawsuit, Dr. Alia Goodheart, testified Friday that Clancy denied having a suicide plan after admitting herself to McLean Hospital over New Year’s Day in 2023.

Advertisement:

Further, she said, Clancy cited “her children and her family, her mother” as reasons to live.

Abby Patkin

Staff Writer

Abby Patkin is a general assignment news reporter whose work touches on public transit, crime, health, and everything in between. She has been covering the Lindsay Clancy murder case since January 2023.
